final_text: HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default (keep-alive), so repeated polls usually reuse one TCP/TLS connection. Only 'Connection: close' or an idle timeout ends it. HTTP/1.0 opened a new connection per request.
note: RFC 9112 9.3: HTTP/1.1 defaults to persistent connections; close option ends it. MDN: HTTP/1.0 default short-lived. Idle timeouts/server limits also end connections ("only" is slightly strong but acceptable).

final_text: TCP closes each direction independently: a FIN from one side is ACKed, then a FIN from the other side is ACKed (four segments), and the side that closed first waits in TIME-WAIT for 2xMSL.
note: RFC 9293 state machine: FIN/ACK each direction, TIME-WAIT with Timeout=2MSL. Can be 3 segments when FIN and ACK combine.

final_text: Keep long-poll timeouts modest: RFC 6202 notes that too-long waits can be cut by proxies with 408/504 and suggests about 30 seconds as a safe value.
note: RFC 6202 (2011, Informational): too-high timeout can produce 408/504; "generally 30 seconds is a safer value". Dated but still standard guidance.

final_text: Amazon SQS exposes long polling as a parameter: ReceiveMessage with WaitTimeSeconds > 0 (max 20 s) returns as soon as a message is available.
note: SQS docs: WaitTimeSeconds > 0 = long polling, max 20 s, returns as soon as messages are available. Duplicate of A-DC-05; keep this one.

final_text: The WebSocket handshake is an HTTP/1.1 GET with 'Upgrade: websocket' and 'Connection: Upgrade'. The server answers '101 Switching Protocols', and from then on the TCP connection carries WebSocket frames.
note: RFC 6455 handshake example: GET + Upgrade: websocket + Connection: Upgrade; 101 Switching Protocols.

final_text: RFC 8441 lets a WebSocket run over a single stream of an HTTP/2 connection (extended CONNECT), so one TCP connection can carry both HTTP/2 requests and WebSockets.
note: RFC 8441: WebSocket over a single HTTP/2 stream via extended CONNECT; other streams can carry normal HTTP/2. Server/browser support varies.

final_text: WebSocket frames have a 2-byte minimum header (up to 14 bytes with extended length and masking), and every client-to-server frame must be masked.
note: RFC 6455 5.1/5.2: client MUST mask all frames; header 2 bytes base, +2/+8 extended length, +4 masking key = 14 max (derived from the frame layout).

final_text: WebSocket defines Ping and Pong control frames, used as keepalives or to check that the peer is still responsive.
note: RFC 6455 5.5.2: Ping "may serve either as a keepalive or as a means to verify that the remote endpoint is still responsive".

final_text: Browsers' EventSource reconnects automatically. On reconnect it sends a Last-Event-ID header with the last 'id:' it saw, so the server can resume the stream. The server can set the delay with a 'retry:' field.
note: WHATWG: Last-Event-ID header set on reconnect; retry field sets reconnection time.

final_text: A server can tell an SSE client to stop reconnecting by responding with HTTP 204 No Content.
note: WHATWG: "a client can be told to stop reconnecting using the HTTP 204 No Content response code".

final_text: Over HTTP/1.1, browsers allow only about 6 concurrent connections per domain, shared across tabs, which SSE streams quickly exhaust. Over HTTP/2 the streams are multiplexed (default ~100).
note: MDN EventSource: limit 6 per browser+domain on HTTP/1.1 ("Won't fix" in Chrome/Firefox); HTTP/2 negotiated, default 100.

final_text: SSE streams use MIME type text/event-stream and must be UTF-8 text. There is no binary framing as in WebSockets.
note: WHATWG: MIME type text/event-stream; "Event streams are always decoded as UTF-8".

final_text: Some proxies, notably legacy ones, drop idle HTTP connections after a short timeout. The SSE spec suggests sending a comment line (starting with ':') about every 15 seconds to keep the stream alive.
note: Spec wording is "Legacy proxy servers are known to, in certain cases, drop HTTP connections after a short timeout".

final_text: Idle timeouts differ by layer: AWS ALB defaults to 60 s, AWS NLB TCP listeners to 350 s, nginx proxy_read_timeout to 60 s. Long-lived connections need heartbeats (e.g. WebSocket pings) or tuned timeouts.
note: ALB idle_timeout default 60 s; NLB TCP default 350 s (TLS listeners fixed at 350 s); nginx closes WebSocket proxy after 60 s with no data unless proxy_read_timeout raised or pings sent.

final_text: An L7 proxy must forward the hop-by-hop Upgrade and Connection headers for a WebSocket to work. nginx does not pass them by default, so they must be set explicitly.
note: nginx: Upgrade is hop-by-hop and not passed; headers must be passed explicitly. Note: nginx >= 1.29.7 no longer needs proxy_http_version 1.1 (per page comment), but Upgrade/Connection headers still must be set.

final_text: With AWS ALB, an upgraded WebSocket becomes a persistent connection between the client and one target through the load balancer, so a single WebSocket is pinned to one backend automatically.
note: Listeners page: upgraded connection "becomes a persistent WebSocket connection between the client and the target". Target-group page adds: "WebSocket connections are inherently sticky ... After the WebSockets upgrade is complete, cookie-based stickiness is not used." Not supported for target groups with target optimizer.

final_text: Socket.IO is not a WebSocket implementation. It adds its own packet metadata and falls back to HTTP long-polling, so a plain WebSocket client cannot connect to a Socket.IO server. Its client reconnects automatically with exponential backoff.
note: Text matches. Source is a W3cubDocs mirror of the Socket.IO v4 docs (2014-2021 snapshot), not socket.io itself; socket.io was unreachable from my environment. Prefer swapping to https://socket.io/docs/v4/ after a manual check.

final_text: Socket.IO's docs: running several Socket.IO servers needs sticky sessions when HTTP long-polling is enabled (the default), because one session spans several HTTP requests; if you use only the WebSocket transport, you don't need them. To broadcast to clients connected to other nodes you also need an adapter that passes messages between servers.
note: Cited index page does not cover sticky sessions or adapters; the multiple-nodes page (mirror) does. It does not name Redis, so "e.g. Redis" was removed. Mirror caveat as A-CM-17.

final_text: Retries during overload make it worse. Add exponential backoff with jitter so reconnects spread out over time instead of arriving as one synchronized storm.
note: AWS Builder Center article (Marc Brooker, modified Jun 2026): retries ineffective if all clients retry at once; jitter spreads arrivals.

final_text: A TCP connection is identified by its 4-tuple (source IP and port, destination IP and port). Ephemeral-port limits constrain the connecting side, while one server port can hold millions of connections; WhatsApp reported over 2 million per server.
note: Cloudflare blog: connection = 4-tuple; ~28k default ephemeral ports limit outgoing connections. WhatsApp blog (Jan 2012) "over 2 million tcp connections" on one box. Should say "WhatsApp reported (2012)".

final_text: QUIC (RFC 9000) is a connection-oriented, stateful transport carried in UDP datagrams, with streams and connection migration. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) runs over it, avoiding TCP head-of-line blocking that affects HTTP/2.
note: RFC 9000: connection-oriented, stateful, packets in UDP datagrams, streams, connection migration. RFC 9114: HTTP/2 multiplexing invisible to TCP loss recovery causes stalls; QUIC per-stream.

final_text: HTTP/2 multiplexes many concurrent requests over one connection, which further reduces per-request connection cost for polling clients.
note: RFC 9113: request multiplexing via independent streams.

final_text: APNs is best-effort: it may reorder notifications, stores only one pending notification per app, and may throttle. Providers should keep HTTP/2 connections to APNs open and reuse them for hours to days.
note: Apple doc: best-effort, may reorder; stores only one notification per bundle ID; may throttle; reuse connection "for many hours to days".

final_text: Google deprecated GCM in April 2018 and said its server and client APIs would be removed as soon as April 11, 2019; Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) replaced it. FCM delivers through platform transport layers: the Android transport layer (devices with Google Play services), APNs for Apple devices, and the Web Push protocol for browsers.
note: Google blog announced removal "as soon as April 11th, 2019" (forward-looking), so "removed starting April 11, 2019" overstates what the source shows. I did not open an official page on the 2023-2024 retirement of FCM legacy APIs (third-party sources say June 2024), so that is not added.

final_text: MQTT is a client/server publish/subscribe protocol that runs over TCP/IP or any ordered, lossless, bi-directional transport. MQTT 5.0 defines WebSocket as one such transport.
note: MQTT 5.0 spec: runs over TCP/IP or other ordered, lossless, bi-directional transports; chapter 6 "Using WebSocket as a network transport".

final_text: PostgreSQL materialized views are not updated automatically: their contents stay as of the last REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW. A plain refresh can block readers; REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY avoids that but requires a unique index on the view.
note: PG docs: refresh replaces contents; non-CONCURRENTLY refresh "could block" readers; CONCURRENTLY needs a UNIQUE index on plain column names covering all rows, and the view must already be populated.

final_text: Oracle can keep materialized views current automatically: with ON COMMIT refresh the view is updated whenever a transaction on the base tables commits, and with ON STATEMENT after every DML statement. Fast refresh applies only the changes instead of recomputing the whole query; ON COMMIT fast refresh relies on materialized view logs, while ON STATEMENT needs none.
note: Original said fast refresh applies changes "recorded in materialized view logs" for both modes; Oracle docs say ON STATEMENT needs no MV logs. Cited page is the 19c guide; behaviour unchanged in later releases as far as checked, but link is version-specific.

final_text: Linux keeps recently read file data in the page cache (RAM), so a 'disk' cache that is read often is actually served from memory. That is a big part of why a local disk cache can beat a remote cache.
note: kernel.org: "Whenever a file is read, the data is put into the page cache to avoid expensive disk access on the subsequent reads." The second sentence is reasonable inference, labeled as such ("a big part of why").

final_text: On AWS, EC2 root volumes normally come from EBS-backed AMIs (AWS recommends them). 'Instance store' disks are physically attached to the host; AWS calls them ideal for buffers, caches and scratch data, and their data does not survive the instance being stopped, hibernated or terminated (it does survive a reboot).
note: Cited page supports physically attached / ideal for caches, but NOT "default root disk is EBS" or "lost when it stops"; those come from the two added AWS pages.

final_text: Classic latency reference numbers (Jeff Dean's list, circa 2012): main-memory reference ~100 ns; random 4 KB SSD read ~150 µs; round trip within the same datacenter ~500 µs. Exact values have moved with newer hardware, but random reads from SSD are still orders of magnitude slower than RAM.
note: Numbers match the gist, which is explicitly "~2012"; must be labeled as dated. Fastly (2015) reports SSD object reads under 500 µs 95% of the time, consistent with the order-of-magnitude point.

final_text: Amazon API Gateway (REST) caches only GET by default, with a default TTL of 300 s (max 3600 s). You can flush a stage's whole cache, and an authorized client can refresh one entry by sending 'Cache-Control: max-age=0'.
note: API Gateway REST caching doc: only GET cached by default, default TTL 300 s, max 3600 s, stage flush, client invalidation with Cache-Control: max-age=0 when authorized (IAM). Applies to REST APIs, not HTTP APIs.

final_text: nginx proxy_cache takes cache lifetime from proxy_cache_valid or from the upstream's X-Accel-Expires / Cache-Control / Expires headers, and by default does not cache responses that set cookies. Purging entries (proxy_cache_purge) is a commercial NGINX Plus feature.
note: nginx proxy module: X-Accel-Expires > Expires/Cache-Control; Set-Cookie responses not cached; proxy_cache_purge "available as part of our commercial subscription".

final_text: Cloudflare does not cache HTML or JSON by default; to cache API responses at the edge you must add a Cache Rule.
note: Cloudflare: "does not cache HTML or JSON by default"; caching is by file extension; use Cache Rules to cache more.

final_text: Mark per-user responses 'Cache-Control: private' so only the browser caches them. Shared caches (CDNs, reverse proxies) may serve anything cacheable to every user.
note: MDN HTTP caching: personalized content must use Cache-Control: private; otherwise shared caches may let other users retrieve it.

final_text: For CDN content that changes, AWS recommends versioned file names over invalidation: users may keep seeing old versions from browser and intermediate caches after an invalidation, and invalidations cost money.
note: CloudFront doc recommends versioning for frequently updated files: after invalidation users may still see old versions from local/corporate caches; versioning is less expensive because you do not pay for invalidations.

final_text: Redis 6+ supports server-assisted client-side caching (CLIENT TRACKING). Redis remembers which keys a client read and sends it an invalidation message when they change. Redis notes the plain pub/sub approach is costly because invalidations go to every client.
note: Redis client-side caching page: Redis 6 Tracking; default mode remembers keys per client; pub/sub approach "costly" since invalidations go to every client. Note Redis also has a broadcasting mode (prefix-based).

final_text: Redis's guidance for local caches is to put a maximum TTL on every locally cached key, even if the source key has none, and to cap local cache memory with an eviction policy.
note: Redis: "Putting a max TTL on every key is a good idea, even if it has no TTL" and "Limiting the amount of memory used by clients is absolutely needed".

final_text: Replica staleness can be measured: on RDS for MySQL the ReplicaLag metric reports Seconds_Behind_Master. With PostgreSQL streaming replication the delay is usually under one second if the standby keeps up.
note: RDS ReplicaLag reports Seconds_Behind_Master; PG docs: streaming replication delay "typically under one second assuming the standby is powerful enough".

final_text: MySQL semisynchronous replication makes the source hold each commit until at least one replica has received and logged the transaction's events. If the source then crashes, every committed transaction has reached at least one replica. The cost is slower commits, and if no replica acknowledges before a timeout, the source reverts to asynchronous replication until a replica catches up.
note: Docs say committed transactions have been "transmitted to at least one replica" (not "survive" in a broader sense); "adds a round trip" is not stated, docs say commits are slower due to waiting. Fallback-to-async confirmed. Page fetched for MySQL 8.4 (LTS).

final_text: On Amazon RDS, a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment keeps a synchronous standby that takes over automatically but can't serve reads (Multi-AZ DB clusters, a different option, do have readable standbys). Read replicas serve reads but are promoted by you, not automatically. Aurora promotes a reader replica automatically on failure, typically in under 60 seconds and often under 30.
note: Original omitted that "Multi-AZ" now has two forms; the cited AWS page itself points to Multi-AZ DB clusters for read traffic. Promotion page describes a manual procedure.

final_text: Built-in read/write routing exists: Aurora's reader endpoint balances connections across replicas, and PostgreSQL's libpq can pick a primary or standby from a host list with target_session_attrs (read-write, standby, prefer-standby).
note: Aurora reader endpoint load-balances connections across replicas; libpq target_session_attrs supports any/read-write/read-only/primary/standby/prefer-standby, plus load_balance_hosts.

final_text: With hash(key) mod N, changing N remaps nearly all keys. Consistent hashing moves only about keys/servers of them on average, which is why shard routers avoid plain modulo.
note: Wikipedia: modular hashing remaps nearly all keys on resize; consistent hashing remaps n/m on average. Wikipedia is acceptable for this textbook fact; Vitess docs (key ranges) are an alternative citation.

final_text: Choose a shard/partition key with many distinct, evenly accessed values (e.g. user ID). Keys with few values or time-bucketed keys (status code, creation date) create hot partitions.
note: DynamoDB partition-key guidance table: user ID good; status code bad; creation date rounded to a period bad. Generalising from DynamoDB to shard keys is reasonable but the page is DynamoDB-specific; the site should say "AWS DynamoDB guidance".

final_text: RDS for MySQL allows up to 15 read replicas per source, and AWS advises giving each replica the same compute and storage as the source so it can keep up.
note: RDS MySQL: up to 15 read replicas per DB instance in a Region; each replica "should have the same amount of compute and storage resources as the source".

final_text: For spikes you know about in advance, EC2 Auto Scaling has scheduled scaling (raise capacity at a set time, e.g. before a campaign goes out). Predictive scaling forecasts recurring daily/weekly patterns and launches capacity ahead of them, and warm pools keep pre-initialized instances (stopped, hibernated or running) ready to join quickly. Reactive scaling alone lags.
note: Predictive scaling is for cyclical/recurring patterns, not a one-off campaign; scheduled scaling is the fit for L-0090/L-0091. Warm pools can be Stopped, Running or Hibernated, not only stopped.

final_text: With ALB sticky sessions, a client keeps going to the same target until the stickiness cookie expires. If that target is deregistered or unhealthy, the ALB picks a new target for the client, so anything the old server cached in memory for that user is lost and must be rebuilt.
note: The "adding many targets leaves load uneven until stickiness is reset" part is not on the cited page (no such text found); dropped. Failover to a new target is stated; "loses its cache" is inference.

final_text: OWASP: don't store session identifiers in localStorage, because any JavaScript on the page can read it. Use cookies with the HttpOnly flag instead.
note: OWASP HTML5 cheat sheet: "Do not store session identifiers in local storage as the data is always accessible by JavaScript. Cookies can mitigate this risk using the httpOnly flag." Applies to JWTs used as bearer/session tokens. (HttpOnly cookies then need CSRF protection; not on this page.)

final_text: localStorage is synchronous and limited to about 5 MiB per origin, and writes past the quota throw QuotaExceededError. MDN recommends IndexedDB for large or performance-sensitive data.
note: MDN: Web Storage is synchronous, 5 MiB local + 5 MiB session per origin, QuotaExceededError; IndexedDB suggested for larger/performance-sensitive data.

final_text: The most common DDoS attacks (UDP reflection, SYN floods) are infrastructure-layer floods that fill network capacity. Mitigating them needs capacity that scales faster than the flood, which application rate limiters don't provide.
note: AWS DDoS whitepaper: UDP reflection and SYN floods are the most common, infrastructure-layer; mitigation needs capacity that scales faster than the flood. "Rate limiters don't provide" is inference, fair.

final_text: The transactional outbox pattern writes the outgoing message into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change, and a separate relay then publishes it to the broker. It avoids 2PC (which many databases and brokers don't support), and a message is sent if and only if the transaction commits. Trade-offs: other services see the change only after the relay runs (eventual, not strong, consistency), and the relay may publish a message more than once, so consumers must be idempotent.
note: "At the cost of eventual consistency" is inference, not stated; the page does state the relay may publish more than once. Overlaps A-DC-22: use this one (attached to L-0363) and merge A-DC-22 into it.

final_text: SQS visibility timeout defaults to 30 seconds and can be set from 0 seconds to 12 hours; a worker can extend it mid-processing with ChangeMessageVisibility (a 'heartbeat'), but never past 12 hours from first receipt.
note: SQS: default 30 s, min 0, max 12 h; ChangeMessageVisibility extends; 12 h limit from first receipt not reset.

final_text: SQS retries are not infinite unless you let them be: a redrive policy's maxReceiveCount moves a message to a dead-letter queue after that many failed receives.
note: SQS DLQ: maxReceiveCount moves message to DLQ. Also relevant to L-0210: for standard queues with maxReceiveCount > 3, a message received 3+ times without deletion is moved to the BACK of the queue.

final_text: SQS standard queues are at-least-once: 'more than one copy of a message might be delivered' and order is best-effort, even within the visibility timeout. Make consumers idempotent.
note: SQS: "more than one copy of a message might be delivered"; best-effort ordering; no guarantee against duplicate delivery "within the visibility timeout period".

final_text: SQS FIFO queues preserve order per MessageGroupId: while one message of a group is in flight, later messages of that group are held back. They also deduplicate (exactly-once processing).
note: SQS FIFO: strict order per message group, later messages of a group held while one is in flight; exactly-once processing; lower TPS (high throughput mode available).

final_text: SQS consumers pull with ReceiveMessage; long polling (WaitTimeSeconds up to 20 s) waits for messages and cuts empty responses and cost.
note: Confirmed, but duplicates A-CM-04; merge.

final_text: RabbitMQ is the opposite: consumers normally subscribe and the broker pushes messages to them. Polling for single messages (basic.get) is called 'highly inefficient' in RabbitMQ's docs and 'strongly recommended against' outside integration tests.
note: Current RabbitMQ docs (4.3) do not use the quoted phrase "highly discouraged"; fixed the quote.

final_text: RabbitMQ Streams (introduced in 3.9, 2021) are an append-only, replicated log with non-destructive reads; consumers can start from the beginning, an offset or a timestamp.
note: RabbitMQ 3.9.0 released 2021-07-23 with Streams; docs: append-only log, non-destructive reads, x-stream-offset (first/last/next/offset/timestamp).

final_text: Kafka's broker default retention is 7 days (log.retention.hours=168, no size limit). Topics can instead use log compaction (cleanup.policy=compact), which keeps the latest record per key.
note: Kafka 4.2 broker configs: log.retention.hours 168, log.retention.bytes -1; cleanup.policy delete default, compact keeps latest value per key. Same in 4.3.

final_text: Kinesis keeps records for 24 hours by default, extendable to 365 days at extra cost.
note: 24 h default, up to 8760 h; pricing page confirms extended and long-term retention are extra charges (added as source).

final_text: Each provisioned Kinesis shard takes up to 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s of writes. For reads it gives 2 MB/s (and 5 GetRecords calls/s) shared by all standard consumers; consumers registered for enhanced fan-out each get their own 2 MB/s. Shard count therefore sets throughput and the maximum parallelism of a consumer application.
note: Original implied 2 MB/s per consumer; pricing page: without enhanced fan-out each shard gives 2 MB/s "regardless of the number of consumers".

final_text: With the Kinesis Client Library, shard-to-worker assignment uses leases tracked in a DynamoDB lease table (each shard's lease is held by one worker at a time; KCL 3.x also creates worker-metrics and coordinator-state tables). Your account pays for these DynamoDB tables.
note: Cited page is for KCL 1.x/2.x ("previous versions"); replaced with current KCL 3.x pages, which also carry the billing warning.

final_text: Kafka 4.0 added 'Queues for Kafka' share groups (KIP-932) as early access; Kafka 4.2 (Feb 2026) made them production-ready (4.3 is the current release). A share group can have more consumers than partitions, with per-record acknowledgements, but records can be delivered out of order.
note: All confirmed. Ordering caveat is from KIP-932 ("records ... can be delivered out of order"), not the design page, so KIP added. Kafka 4.3.1 (June 2026) is the latest supported release per kafka.apache.org/community/downloads.

final_text: Kafka 4.0 made the KIP-848 consumer group protocol generally available: assignment moves to the broker and 'stop-the-world' rebalances go away. Clients opt in with group.protocol=consumer; the default is still classic as of Kafka 4.3.
note: Checked 4.3 consumer configs: default still classic. Updated version reference.

final_text: Adding partitions doesn't move existing data, and keyed records may start going to a different partition, which 'may disturb consumers' relying on it. Kafka cannot reduce a topic's partition count.
note: Kafka ops docs: adding partitions does not move data, "may disturb consumers"; "Kafka does not currently support reducing the number of partitions".

final_text: Records with no key don't get hashed: the default producer uses a 'sticky' partition and switches after about batch.size bytes.
note: Producer configs: no key -> sticky partition that changes when at least batch.size bytes produced.

final_text: Producer-side ordering within a partition relies on idempotence (enable.idempotence=true by default). With idempotence off and more than 1 in-flight request, retries can reorder records.
note: Producer configs: idempotence default true unless conflicting configs; with idempotence false and max.in.flight > 1, retries may reorder.

final_text: Kafka's docs: at-least-once by default; at-most-once by committing before processing; exactly-once via transactional producers + read_committed consumers for Kafka-to-Kafka processing. Exactly-once into external systems 'generally requires cooperation' from them.
note: Kafka design: transactional producer + read_committed give exactly-once for Kafka-to-Kafka; other destinations "generally requires cooperation"; at-least-once by default.

final_text: enable.auto.commit defaults to true with a 5 s interval. It gives at-least-once only if you finish processing each poll() batch before the next poll; otherwise records can be skipped.
note: enable.auto.commit default true, auto.commit.interval.ms 5000; KafkaConsumer javadoc: auto-commit gives at-least-once only if all records from each poll are consumed before the next poll/close, else committed offset can get ahead.

final_text: A Kafka consumer's position per partition is one integer (the next offset to read), so it is cheap to checkpoint, and a consumer can rewind to an older offset to reprocess data.
note: Kafka design: position is "just a single integer"; acknowledgements cheap; consumer can rewind to re-consume.

final_text: Pricing dimensions: SQS bills per request, with each 64 KB chunk of payload counted as one request (first 1 million requests a month free). Kinesis has three modes: provisioned bills per shard-hour plus PUT payload units (25 KB chunks); On-demand Standard bills per GB written and read plus a per-stream hourly charge; On-demand Advantage bills per GB written and read with no stream-hour charge but an account-level minimum (25 MB/s in and out). Extended retention and enhanced fan-out cost extra.
note: Kinesis pricing page now lists three modes (On-demand Standard, On-demand Advantage, Provisioned). Advantage details (no fixed stream-hour charge; account-level minimum of 25 MB/s ingested and retrieved) taken from the pricing page; prices change, so link rather than quote figures.

final_text: SNS FIFO topics can archive messages for 1 to 365 days and replay them to subscriptions, narrowing the replay gap between SNS+SQS and Kafka.
note: SNS FIFO archive 1-365 days, replay to subscriptions, extra charges. FIFO topics only.

final_text: When a service must both update its DB and publish an event, the transactional outbox pattern writes the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction and a relay publishes it, avoiding 2PC. Consumers must still be idempotent.
note: Confirmed (same page as A-CS-25, both URL forms serve identical content). Duplicate; merge with A-CS-25.

final_text: Elasticsearch search is near real-time: indexes refresh every 1 s by default (only on indices searched in the last 30 s), so a newly indexed blog may not be searchable instantly.
note: Elastic: refresh every second, only on indices that received a search in the last 30 s; "within 1 second" otherwise.

final_text: PostgreSQL's default isolation is READ COMMITTED. UPDATE ... SET claps = claps + 1 applies to the latest committed row version, so concurrent claps aren't lost; read-then-write in application code needs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or a stricter isolation level.
note: PG: Read Committed default; concurrent UPDATE waits and applies to the updated row version; SELECT FOR UPDATE locks.

final_text: A semaphore 'initialized to one' (a binary semaphore) acts as a mutual-exclusion lock; for a plain counter, an atomic increment such as Java's AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() needs no lock at all.
note: Java Semaphore doc: semaphore initialized to one = binary semaphore, usable as mutual exclusion lock. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet is atomic (java.util.concurrent.atomic is the lock-free toolkit). Java 21 docs; same API in later JDKs.
